issues.legal_issue: Testimony from witnesses related to the victims may be accepted as credible despite the absence of independent witnesses when it withstands careful scrutiny and is corroborated by the contemporaneous report.
material_facts: The prosecution relied principally on two eyewitnesses, both of whom were related to the victims.
Their accounts agreed on the material details and were consistent with the promptly lodged report, which named the accused and described their roles.
Cross-examination did not reveal material infirmities in their testimony.
Although other people were present in the area, no independent witness came forward to assist the prosecution.
issues.conclusion: The eyewitnesses’ relationship to the victims did not justify rejecting their testimony; the testimony was trustworthy and supported the convictions.
issues.legal_principle: A witness's close relationship to a victim does not by itself discredit the witness. The court must scrutinize such evidence with utmost care and caution; the judgment cites no earlier case for this principle.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_conviction and related_eyewitnesses and consistent_accounts and prompt_report_corrobates_accounts and cross_examination_reveals_no_material_infirmity

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The accused appealed criminal convictions based on the prosecution evidence.
predicates.related_eyewitnesses: The principal eyewitnesses were close relatives of the victims.
predicates.consistent_accounts: The eyewitnesses gave accounts that agreed on the material details of the occurrence.
predicates.prompt_report_corrobates_accounts: A report made soon after the occurrence named the accused and corroborated the eyewitnesses’ accounts.
predicates.cross_examination_reveals_no_material_in: Cross-examination did not disclose a material defect that undermined the eyewitnesses’ credibility.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a conviction based on related eyewitnesses, their testimony is accepted as credible if their accounts are consistent, promptly corroborated, and not materially undermined in cross-examination.

issues.legal_issue: Delay in forwarding a promptly lodged report and minor investigative omissions do not, without more, make the report or prosecution case unreliable.
material_facts: The report was lodged within hours of the occurrence and the police reached the scene that night and began investigating.
The copy of the report was delayed in reaching the local magistrate, and the crime title was omitted from the inquest reports.
The record did not show that the investigating officer antedated the documents or fabricated the investigation.
issues.conclusion: The procedural irregularities did not undermine the report or the otherwise credible prosecution evidence.
issues.legal_principle: A delay in forwarding a report or a minor omission in investigative documents must be assessed in the context of the whole record; it does not displace positive, credible evidence merely by its existence. The judgment cites no earlier case for this principle.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_conviction and prompt_report_lodged and investigation_began_promptly and forwarding_delay_or_minor_omission and no_evidence_of_fabrication

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The accused appealed criminal convictions that the prosecution supported with a report and investigation records.
predicates.prompt_report_lodged: A report describing the occurrence was lodged soon after it happened.
predicates.investigation_began_promptly: Investigators reached the scene and began investigative steps soon after the report was made.
predicates.forwarding_delay_or_minor_omission: The report was forwarded late or an investigative document contained a minor omission.
predicates.no_evidence_of_fabrication: The evidence did not show that investigators fabricated or antedated the report or related records.

issues.definition: A report remains usable despite a forwarding delay or minor omission when it was promptly lodged, the investigation began promptly, and there is no evidence of fabrication.

issues.legal_issue: Members of an unlawful assembly may be held responsible for murders committed in prosecution of its common object when the evidence establishes that the assembly’s object included those murders.
material_facts: The accused acted together as an armed group against members of a family whom they believed were sheltering persons suspected of killing one of the accused’s relatives.
After the suspected persons were not found, the group continued the attack, fired on victims, restrained them, severed the heads of three victims, and threw a child into a fire.
The attack was sustained and coordinated, and the manner of the killings supported the finding that the group intended mass murder as well as revenge.
issues.conclusion: The common object of the unlawful assembly included committing mass murders, and the convictions for murder with the aid of the rule of common-object liability were upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code, members of an unlawful assembly may be liable for offences committed in prosecution of its common object. The object may be inferred from the assembly’s conduct and may develop during the occurrence. The Court considered Shambhu Nath Singh v. State of Bihar, Bhudeo Mandal v. State of Bihar, and Raghubir Singh v. State of Punjab, but held their ratios inapplicable on these facts.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The accused appealed convictions arising from an alleged group offence.
predicates.unlawful_assembly_proved: The evidence established that the accused acted together as an unlawful assembly.
predicates.coordinated_attack_continued_after_initi: The group continued its coordinated attack even after the persons it initially sought were not found.
predicates.attack_evidence_shows_common_object_incl: The group’s conduct, including coordinated killings and extreme violence, showed that its common object included murder.

issues.definition: Members of a proved unlawful assembly are liable for murders in prosecution of its common object when the group continues a coordinated attack after its initial object fails and its conduct shows that murder formed part of its common object.

issues.legal_issue: An alibi is not established merely by evidence that an accused’s children studied in another locality when that evidence does not show that the accused was there at the time of the offence.
material_facts: Two accused relied on evidence that their children attended a college in another locality and asserted that they lived there.
The witnesses did not establish that the accused themselves were residing there at the time of the occurrence.
No other evidence was led to establish their absence from the scene.
issues.conclusion: The evidence did not establish the alibis, and the convictions were not disturbed on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: An alibi must be established on the evidence; proof that an accused’s children studied elsewhere does not, without evidence of the accused’s own presence there, establish the accused’s absence from the scene. The Court assessed the evidence on the stated standard of preponderance of probability and cited no earlier case for this application.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_conviction and alibi_claimed and evidence_shows_children_studied_elsewhere and no_evidence_places_accused_elsewhere_at_offence_time

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The accused appealed a criminal conviction and relied on an alibi.
predicates.alibi_claimed: The accused asserted that they were elsewhere when the offence occurred.
predicates.evidence_shows_children_studied_elsewher: Evidence showed that the accused’s children studied in another locality.
predicates.no_evidence_places_accused_elsewhere_at_: The evidence did not establish that the accused themselves were elsewhere when the offence occurred.

issues.definition: An alibi is not established when the accused relies on proof that their children studied elsewhere but offers no evidence placing the accused elsewhere at the time of the offence.

issues.legal_issue: A death sentence must be reduced where the evidence does not conclusively establish the individual role relied on to distinguish the accused for capital punishment, even though the accused remains liable as a member of the unlawful assembly.
material_facts: One accused was said to have fired at a child who was then thrown into a fire by other assailants.
The child’s autopsy disclosed no pellet, no pellet was recovered from the ashes, and the child’s charred body did not permit identification of an injury.
The accused’s presence, membership in the unlawful assembly, and participation in the armed attack were nevertheless proved.
issues.conclusion: The death sentence was reduced to life imprisonment, while the murder conviction with the aid of Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code and the other convictions were left undisturbed.
issues.legal_principle: Capital sentencing requires individual consideration of the accused’s proved role; an accused whose specific role is not established conclusively may receive different treatment from other participants. The Court applied the common-object rule in Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code and considered the capital-sentencing principles discussed in Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab, Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab, and Allauddin Mian v. State of Bihar.

predicates.appeal_against_death_sentence: The accused appealed a sentence of death.
predicates.accused_role_evidence_is_inconclusive_on: The evidence did not conclusively establish the particular act relied on to distinguish the accused for capital punishment.
predicates.unlawful_assembly_participation_and_comm: The accused’s participation in an unlawful assembly and liability for its common object were proved.

issues.definition: A death sentence is reduced when the evidence of the accused’s particular aggravating act is inconclusive, even though the accused’s participation and common-object liability are proved.

issues.legal_issue: The death penalty is justified in a rarest-of-rare case when the aggravating circumstances of the crime and the offenders outweigh the mitigating circumstances and leave no adequate alternative.
material_facts: Six accused appealed death sentences for their roles in a coordinated attack in which five people were killed.
The murders were pre-planned and exceptionally brutal: three victims were beheaded, and a child was thrown into a fire and burned alive.
The offenders carried the severed heads in a procession and proclaimed victory.
The Court considered the proposed mitigating circumstances but found that they were outweighed by the scale and brutality of the crime, its motive, and the offenders’ conduct.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the case fell within the rarest-of-rare category and upheld the death sentences of the six accused.
issues.legal_principle: Life imprisonment is the rule and death is an exception; death may be imposed only in the rarest of rare cases when the alternative option is unquestionably foreclosed. The court must balance aggravating and mitigating circumstances and consider both the crime and the criminal. The Court relied on Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab, Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab, and Allauddin Mian v. State of Bihar.

predicates.appeal_against_death_sentence: The accused appealed sentences of death.
predicates.multiple_murders_committed_with_extreme_: The offenders committed multiple murders in an exceptionally brutal manner.
predicates.conduct_shows_planning_and_exceptional_c: The manner of the attack showed planning and exceptional cruelty, including extreme violence against a child.
predicates.aggravating_circumstances_outweigh_mitig: After considering both sides, the court found the aggravating circumstances outweighed the mitigating circumstances.

issues.definition: A death sentence is upheld as a rarest-of-rare ruling when an appeal concerns multiple exceptionally brutal murders, the conduct shows planning and exceptional cruelty, and the aggravating circumstances outweigh the mitigating circumstances.
